pageCache.pageTitle: How do humans learn, and what does that mean for educational policy? - Winchester College | Independent Boarding School
pageCache.text:
How do humans learn, and what does that mean for educational policy?
In her latest video to parents, Headmaster, Ms Elizabeth Stone spoke about what we know, and what we don’t, about human learning based on the findings of cognitive psychologists. One of the fundamental principles is that the more knowledge you start with, the more easily you will learn or, put another way, the efficiency of learning is dramatically affected by background knowledge.
“If the quality of learning is a function of how much you already know, there are significant implications for education and education policy”
Ms Stone commented: “If the quality of learning is a function of how much you already know, there are significant implications for education and education policy. First, those who are serious about maximising learning need to structure the curriculum really carefully. For children to learn at higher levels they must first be taught a broad, well-integrated base of background knowledge relevant to the subject. But this isn’t easy: if you make the curriculum narrow but very deep, then the benefit of having prior knowledge is tightly constrained.
“You can’t, for instance, just dedicate all your time to Maths and English, because the background knowledge acquired through History and Geography and Music and Languages and Science all helps children grasp new ideas about the world. Intelligent judgements have to be made, not just about whether particular knowledge is valuable (all knowledge is valuable), but about what can intentionally be used as building blocks.”
How do humans learn
Please accept cookies to enable video playback. Manage cookie settings
“This is yet another advantage of Div. Because we can use it to introduce seminal ideas that provide a conceptual framework that underpins further learning across the curriculum.”
Ms Stone continues: “But there are too many good things in the world to teach all of them in school. A more realistic approach is to accept that we are preparing young people for a lifelong exploration of the world, and that our job is to give them an excellent start. We don’t have to beat ourselves up for not delivering the end product by the age of 18.
“This is yet another advantage of Div. Because we can use it to introduce seminal ideas that provide a conceptual framework that underpins further learning across the curriculum. And the versatility and flexibility that come from being unexamined make it more useful than, say, doing another A-level or GCSE which is tightly constrained by the exam syllabus.
“Good educational policy is going to have to confront this challenge, rather than pretending that there is no opportunity cost.”
“The second implication for educational policy is that we need to be careful about how much of life-skills we try to fit into the timetable. There are endless calls for schools to deliver life skills, but the public debate never addresses the obvious question of what should be displaced to make room. Good educational policy is going to have to confront this challenge, rather than pretending that there is no opportunity cost.
“But in the meantime, here at Winchester, we are clear that doing the most important things well entails doing less of the rest, as good as those things are.”
You can watch the video in full here.

The Arts
At Winchester, pupils are offered a rich variety of creative opportunities across Art, Design & Technology, and Drama. Whether pursuing personal projects or academic goals, pupils benefit from exceptional facilities, expert staff, and a vibrant programme of activities.
Creative Learning
All pupils in Year 9 are introduced to core artistic disciplines including painting, drawing, and printmaking.
Those with a practical or technical focus may explore Design & Technology, solving real-world design and engineering challenges.
Pupils can specialise in a wide range of disciplines such as ceramics, film installations, fashion design, silversmithing, and more. They can also join a variety of arts clubs and societies to further hone their skills.
Competitions such as the Drew Jug Art Competition, and Ingenuity Challenge encourage creativity, cultural exploration, and house collaboration. These competitions inspire pupils to innovate and celebrate artistic achievement.
Specialist Facilities
Art School
Spacious studios and gallery dedicated to painting, printmaking, sculpture, and more. A well-stocked library and access to historic art collections enhance pupils’ creative exploration.
Mill (Design & Technology Centre)
A cutting-edge workshop with 3D printers, electronics labs, and professional software allows pupils to bring innovative designs to life.
QEII Theatre
A fully equipped theatre hosting numerous productions, with opportunities in acting, directing, technical theatre, and stagecraft.
Performing Arts
Drama at Winchester is dynamic and inclusive, with up to ten productions a year and frequent collaborations with local schools.
Pupils take on roles both on stage and behind the scenes, gaining valuable experience in teamwork, time management, and creative leadership.
Drama is also a vehicle for community engagement, from entertaining care home residents to mentoring primary school pupils.

With a choral tradition spanning 600 years, Winchester offers a truly unique musical experience. Two-thirds of our pupils participate in a wide range of musical activities, with opportunities to perform both individually and in groups at every level.
Events this term
Celebrating talent & originality at every level
Music is at the heart of life at Winchester, where several hundred pupils master 25 different instruments under the guidance of dedicated music teachers.
Each week, the school resonates to the sound of 18 ensembles, 10 choirs and hundreds of individual music lessons, creating a diverse musical landscape from classical piano, viol consort, close harmony singing to jazz improvisation and rock bands.
Renowned for excellence, Winchester’s music programme is embedded through Div, concert trips and house events. Pupils’ musical development is nurtured from any starting point, whether picking up an instrument for the first time or preparing for a national audition or diploma.
With purpose-built facilities, outstanding teachers, and an ethos of celebrating talent at all levels, every Wykehamist will leave the school able to call themselves a musician.
Music Awards are available to any candidate who shows exceptional musical achievement and potential and is keen to contribute to the musical life of the school. Dedicated choral and organ scholarships are also available at 16+.
Find out more
Exceptional achievements & experiences
Our purpose-built Music School features 55 teaching rooms accessible to pupils every day.
We have several dedicated performance venues, regular use of Winchester Cathedral and strong connections with King’s College Cambridge and New College Oxford amongst many other prestigious institutions.
Currently, 35 pupils hold at least one music diploma, a Winchester trombonist is a member of the National Youth Orchestra of Great Britain and there is a regular flow of choral and organ scholars to Oxbridge.
The most recent winner of our Concerto Competition performed Shostakovich Cello Concerto No. 2 and Tchaikovsky’s Rococo Variations with the orchestra.
“I have been bowled over by the creativity and inspirational teaching of music at Winchester College. The high calibre of faculty and the individual attention they give their students is world class.”
Rooted in a choral tradition
Over 600 years old, the choral tradition permeates a Winchester education and singing of all kinds abounds.
The Quiristers form an integral part of the Chapel Choir and are boarders between the ages of 9 and 13 at The Pilgrims’ School, a boys-only prep school located next to Winchester College.
Most Quiristers continue to Winchester College, forming a core of expert musicians along with the many Cathedral choristers who choose Winchester.

‘Best for Music’ – The Week Schools Guide 2024

Sixth Form pupil, Laurie, recently earned his piano Fellowship Diploma from Trinity College London.
The diploma is only available to those who have worked through grades 1-8 on their chosen instrument and is equivalent in standard to a postgraduate course recital at a conservatoire or university.
For the last two years, Nye has been a part of the National Youth Orchestra participating in multiple tours across the UK and playing in venues such as the Barbican and the Royal Albert Hall, the latter as part of the BBC Proms.

pageCache.pageTitle: Winchester College appoints first ever Sixth Form Girls' Housemistress - Winchester College | Independent Boarding School
pageCache.text:
Winchester College appoints first ever Sixth Form Girls’ Housemistress
The College is delighted to announce the appointment of Mrs Katherine Cole as the Housemistress of the first Sixth Form Girls’ Boarding House, due to open in September 2026.
I look forward to welcoming Sixth Form girl boarders to a school with over 600 years of history and a deeply embedded culture of manners, kindness, and acceptance.
Katherine joins Winchester from Sherborne Girls in Dorset, where she spent four years as Housemistress of the school’s Upper Sixth house. She studied German and Linguistics at Jesus College, Oxford, and spent a year at the Universität Trier in Germany focusing on German Literature. She qualified as a teacher while working at Hurstpierpoint College, where she also served as Assistant Housemistress.
Her career has included roles as Head of German at both Ardingly College and St. Edward’s School in Oxford, where she was also Assistant Housemistress in the Upper Sixth house and a mixed age house respectively at both schools. Before moving to Sherborne Girls Katherine also taught at Headington School.
Beyond the classroom, Katherine has managed netball and badminton teams, accompanied numerous Duke of Edinburgh expeditions, and led overseas trips and exchanges. She is a particular fan of German Christmas markets and enjoys participating in choirs whenever possible, as well as playing the flute and baritone saxophone. An avid concertgoer and traveler, she moves to Winchester with her two children and her husband, Ben, a Classics teacher.
Commenting on her appointment, Katherine said: “I’m thrilled to be part of this exciting phase in the College’s long history. I look forward to welcoming Sixth Form girl boarders to a school with over 600 years of history and a deeply embedded culture of manners, kindness, and acceptance.”
Take a virtual tour below of one of our two new Sixth Form girls’ boarding houses and get a sense of what it might be like to be among its first residents.

We believe in nurturing pupils who demonstrate outstanding ability, potential, and commitment to music. Talented pupils benefit from expert teaching and tutoring, outstanding facilities, and meaningful support throughout their time at the College.
Audition Process
Winchester offers Music Scholarships and Music Exhibitions at both 13+ and 16+, and Choral and Organ Scholarships for 16+ entries.
All awards are given for performances heard at audition. The audition includes a 15-minute performance, and 10 minutes of practical tests. Informal pre-auditions are also available for all candidates.
In making awards, we are looking for musicianship, potential and commitment, alongside achievement.
Music Awards do not automatically carry a remission on school fees.
Recent Music Success
13+ Music Awards
All Music Award applications for 13+ entry are made at the start of Year 8. Generally, successful 13+ candidates will be at least Grade 6 (or an equivalent) on their first instrument.
If you have already completed a Registration Form for the Admissions Department, please complete Form 1:
13+ Music Award Form 1
If you have not yet registered with the Admissions Department and would like to both register and apply for a Music Award, please complete Form 2:
13+ Music Award Form 2
The deadline for 13+ Music Award applications is the 16th November 2026 for entry in September 2027.
13+ Music Award Guide
16+ Music Awards
Applications for 16+ entry are made at the time of applying to the school.
For 16+ the expectation is that pupils will be Grade 8+ standard, and pupils offering only piano should be of diploma standard.
16+ Music Award
16+ Music Award Application Form
16+ Choral Scholarships
Choral scholar applicants do not need to have taken grades in singing exams but should have experience of regular choral singing. This is an ideal preparation for university choral scholarships and would suit singers who wish to improve their sight-reading and musicianship skills through rehearsing several times per week. Choral scholars must be prepared to commit to services, concerts, tours and broadcasts and will receive 1 to 1 lessons from experienced singing teachers.
It is envisaged that in time, the choral scholars will sing as a small group as well as within the liturgical choirs at Winchester. There will be opportunities to develop singing beyond Winchester through participation in events in Cambridge and Oxford, and for the right applicants, the opportunity to spend a gap year in Winchester working with both the Cathedral and College and pursuing particular musical interests.
Applications are welcomed from all voice parts.
16+ Organ Scholarships
The organ scholars work alongside the Chapel Organist providing organ music for services. They accompany choirs on piano and organ and are able to develop choral (and orchestral) conducting.
Winchester College Chapel Choir with its 16 Quiristers (8–13-year-old trebles) provides an unparalleled opportunity to experience a Cathedral-style training during the Sixth Form, invaluable for organists wishing to apply for university scholarships which involve working with children.

pageCache.pageTitle: Sixth Form pupils win at International Math Challenge in New York - Winchester College | Independent Boarding School
pageCache.text:
Sixth Form pupils win at International Math Challenge in New York
Congratulations to Sixth Form pupils, Alex Cirstea, Victor Sim, Henry Ng, Andrei Diachuk and Yuyao Xie on their outstanding achievement at the MathWorks M3 Challenge in New York yesterday.
Competing against 794 teams, made up of more than 3,600 pupils from across the United States and UK, the team was awarded the Technical Computing Prize for the best use of computer programming, along with a $3,000 cheque. The prize money will be split between the team members and paid directly to their universities next year to offset fees.
“What makes the M3 challenge unique is its emphasis on not just predictions, but also using those predictions to design real solutions.”
To reach the final, the team spent 14 consecutive hours writing a paper which used modelling and computational methods to solve real world problems. This year’s problem was about predicting heatwaves and mitigating their impact on power grids. Their final paper, consisting of over 60 pages, was selected as one of the 3 finalist papers after enduring rigorous examination by the professional judges.
Ahead of their win, the team commented: ‘What makes the M3 challenge unique is its emphasis on not just predictions, but also using those predictions to design real solutions. We prioritised this on Challenge weekend, using domain knowledge of physical and social sciences to make our approaches fresh but still anchored in reality. As a result, we not only predicted trends, but found creative solutions and strategies to solve the problems of tomorrow.’

pageCache.pageTitle: AI, learning and the importance of intellectual ‘friction’  - Winchester College | Independent Boarding School
pageCache.text:
AI, learning and the importance of intellectual ‘friction’
In her latest message to parents, the Headmaster of Winchester College, Ms Elizabeth Stone addressed one of the most topical subjects in education, the role of artificial intelligence in learning. Her remarks explored the foundations of learning, the difference between process and product, and the risks of cognitive offloading in a digital age.
Watch the video below:
AI in education
Please accept cookies to enable video playback. Manage cookie settings
Ms Stone highlighted the importance of sustaining the disciplines of reading, writing, and problem solving, arguing that these practices build the intellectual resilience that AI cannot replace.
Reading builds intellectual stamina – the very opposite of the attentional havoc wreaked by watching 25-second videos for hours a day. And attention is fundamental to learning.
She emphasised that writing remains one of the most powerful tools for developing thought:
“Committing things to paper extends our working memory and allows us to develop more complicated ideas. The writer of anything of substance must read widely, produce a conceptual framework, find the right words, wrestle with syntax and organise the logic of their arguments.”
Ms Stone explained that the educational value of school lies not in the finished product, but in the cognitive effort that the process demands:
Pupils aren’t asked to solve maths problems because the teacher doesn’t know the answer. They aren’t asked to write essays on Macbeth because the world needs more 1500 word analyses by teenagers. We ask them to write because the process develops their minds.
Addressing the rise of AI tools, she drew an analogy with high-tech running shoes, warning that using AI too early or too often risks weakening essential mental muscles:
“I think of AI like those running shoes with carbon fibre springs in the sole. If someone like me trains in them daily, my legs will adjust to the extra power and become weaker. But if someone like Mo Farah pounds out the miles in normal shoes for years, and then pulls on the carbon fibre shoes on race day, he’ll get a world-beating boost.”
She concluded that while AI is new, the core principles of learning are not.
“How we learn is determined by the fundamental structures of the brain, so whilst AI is a new technology, the guard rails on its educational uses are clear. The most reliable way to use it is to introduce it later rather than earlier – when the foundations of knowledge are solid and thinking skills are fluent.”
Her message ended with a reminder that meaningful learning cannot be automated:
“There’s no shortcut: learning deeply requires friction and effort. Schools must not copy workplaces by using AI to produce a better product with as little effort as possible. That effort you just eliminated? That’s the learning.”

pageCache.pageTitle: Winchester College welcomes pupils from across the county for the Hampshire Climate Conference - Winchester College | Independent Boarding School
pageCache.text:
Winchester College welcomes pupils from across the county for the Hampshire Climate Conference
The annual Hampshire Climate Conference recently took place at Winchester College and was attended by more than 200 pupils and teachers from 15 local schools. Participants took part in a wide variety of different workshops by the Final Straw Foundation, Wessex Rivers Trust, the University of Southampton, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Wildlife Trust, as well as pupils from the College’s Sustainability Society.
Sessions from the Final Straw Foundation on sustainable packaging and plastic pollution highlighted the importance of protecting our seas from pollution. A workshop on grassroots adaptations to climate change challenged students to identify a climate, environmental or coastal change and discuss what the impacts were, who is affected and who has the power to make a change. There was also a climate change card sort, sampling of river invertebrates and ecological surveys.
The Hampshire and Isle of Wight Wildlife Trust led an ecology based escape room that considered the effects on river ecology, while pupils from the Winchester College Sustainability Society led a development trading game which allowed students to explore issues in an interactive way.
The event also welcomed guest speakers, Arun Curson and Gareth Boyes who both inspired the pupils to make a difference.
Arun Curson is a Wildlife Trust Young Changemaker Award Winner and he talked about his voluntary work monitoring coastal wildlife. He encouraged participants to make a difference by volunteering with their local wildlife organisations.
Gareth Boyes from Hampshire Youth Parliament compiled a video using humour to get across the importance of taking action to prevent further warming and climate change. This included footage at climate rallies and interviews with young people who are committed to making a difference.
Our thanks go to the Hampshire Youth Parliament volunteers who helped the day run so smoothly and facilitated the workshops.

Learning
Curriculum
At Winchester, academic excellence is driven by deep curiosity and genuine love of learning. An education here combines a rigorous curriculum of examined subjects, taught by expert subject specialists, with the unique cultural and philosophical exploration offered through Div.
GCSE
Pupils in Year 9 study:
Div, Mathematics, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, French and/or German, Geography, History, Latin and Religious Studies.
One language: Ancient Greek, Spanish or Russian.
Two creative subjects: Art, Design & Technology, Computer Science or Music
For GCSEs, all pupils take: English Language, Mathematics, French or German and two or three Sciences, in addition to Div.
In addition, pupils choose from a broad range of subjects including: Latin, History, Geography, Ancient Greek, Art, Design & Technology, Music, Computer Science, Religious Studies, French, German, Spanish and Russian.
A full list of examined subjects can be found below.
A-Level
Pupils study three A-Level subjects plus Div, with the option of additional A-Levels if eligible.
Pupils can also choose to complete an Extended Project Qualification (EPQ), which enables them to explore their cross-curricular interests more deeply and further develop independent research and study skills.
A full list of examined subjects can be found below.
All teachers in the department are practising, exhibited artists. We have talks from visiting experts, an artist-in-residence each year and a regular exhibition programme, which pupils have recently started to curate. Class sizes are small, allowing for a flexible curriculum that is shaped to individual progress. We often use the school’s landscapes, architecture and collections for projects. Inspiration from other subjects, particularly Div, regularly informs lessons and takes us on unexpected tangents.
The extensive facilities in Art School allow pupils to specialise in printmaking, sculpture, painting, drawing or ceramics. Pupils go on to prestigious Art Schools such as St Martin’s, The Ruskin Oxford and to Cambridge to read Architecture. Pupils enjoy extensive access to Art School, so that when they become invested in the subject they can be as ambitious and productive as possible during their time here.
Art History is a research-based subject. It teaches pupils to formulate their own questions in front of a work of art, and to seek the answers independently. Pupils learn to identify imaginatively with distant cultures. They also learn the danger of making assumptions before acquiring knowledge and understanding. Art History requires pupils to look carefully, to think cautiously, and to write with precision.
We are fortunate to have superb works of art to study here on campus and nearby at Winchester Cathedral. In addition to the school’s fine medieval buildings, the art collections include Ancient Greek and Chinese ceramics, medieval sculpture and stained glass, illuminated manuscripts, casts of Renaissance sculpture, English watercolours and 20th century artists’ books. Many Old Wykehamists, such as Stephen Bann, Tim Wilson, Christopher Rowell and Guy Peppiatt, have gone on to become prominent in the art world.
Biology provides a vital grounding in how living processes work as part of a functioning world. The dons use prior experience in agriculture and fisheries and game management to make the learning as pertinent as possible. Pupils also conduct ecology practical work in the school grounds, including the biodiverse River Itchen, and the adjacent National Park, whenever possible.
Pupils are frequently stretched and challenged with material beyond the curriculum, which provides strong preparation for university. Biology students become skilled at lateral thinking, problem solving and possess academic resilience. Many go on to become doctors, vets, and research scientists in the biological sciences. Promising biologists become keen advocates of our popular Natural History Society.A central feature of Winchester’s intellectual life is our year-round programme of society meetings, where leading thinkers, public figures, and subject specialists visit the school to share their expertise and provoke discussion.
With the emphasis on practical work, pupils undertake at least one experimental activity per week. Each chemistry lab contains at least six fume cupboards, allowing paired practical work on organic synthesis. The instrument suite has an FT-IR spectrometer, ultraviolet-visible spectrometers and a gel chromatograph. These instruments are used by pupils in lesson time and for voluntary project work.
Dons seek to provide extra opportunities for pupils of all abilities and ages. We are particularly successful in national competitions such as the Cambridge Chemistry Challenge for Sixth Form pupils, and the UK and International Chemistry Olympiads.
Pupils benefit from the many Scientific Clubs and Societies on offer.
Classics is the foundation of much of Western ideology, culture and language. Winchester has a centuries-strong reputation for this subject, now reinforced by an appropriately contemporary approach.
The focus is unashamedly linguistic: Latin is compulsory up to GCSE and Ancient Greek is also studied. A close reading of ancient texts teaches pupils how to think critically about sources, enhancing skills in analysis and evaluation. Classics is not just the study of linguistics, but also of archaeology, history, politics, law, art and architecture. Pupils have the opportunity to study Greek art in the school’s Treasury, handling 2,500 year-old vases and curating their own exhibitions.
Keen Classicists enjoy the school’s Historical Clubs and Societies.
Computer Science is increasingly important as societies use and reliance on it grows. Pupils must be equipped with the necessary skills to succeed and excel in workplaces that may not even exist yet.
Digital skills and computing topics are taught in the First Year and include skills such as programming, ethics of AI, use of standard applications and digital world education. The GCSE builds on these topics with the opportunity to apply the theoretical elements through programming, robotics and microcontrollers use. Pupils visit the National Museum of Computing at Bletchley for the GCSE course and various societies such as CompSoc provide space for enquiry and competition as well as lectures. Overseas trips are planned with the aim to inspire awareness of exciting career pathways.
Each member of the Design and Technology department comes from a different design or engineering background. Regular visits to museums, engineering firms, as well as large and small factories, inspire individual projects within the curriculum. Learning is tailored to a pupil’s own interests and provides the freedom to explore ideas to fruition.
DT teaches life skills. Pupils are allowed to make mistakes in a controlled environment, overcoming issues independently and understanding how to avoid problems in the future. They are encouraged to avoid thinking in a linear fashion, but to evaluate, make decisions and understand people – ultimately, clients – from whom pupils also receive external briefs. Talented students have gone on to enjoy careers as architects, designers and entrepreneurs; some have read Nuclear Science and Engineering at MIT.
Our various Clubs and Societies are available to all pupils.
Learning to improve the standard of living for ourselves and future generations is in keeping with the school’s philosophy of leadership to serve society. Pupils listen to their peers with respect and accept differences of opinion, quickly learning to compromise with opposing views. Together with an expectation of independent learning, these class discussions are solid preparation for a university education.
Economics can be for anyone, though an aptitude for Maths helps. It is more important to be interested in constructing arguments and counter-arguments, and in current affairs. The department’s own resources, used for much of the course, are kept as up-to-date and relevant as possible. Economics instils a broad range of highly transferable skills, from learning to read data effectively, to avoiding ‘fake news’, to constructing a coherent argument based on potentially conflicting pieces of evidence.
Talented economists appreciate the many Oratorical Clubs and Societies we offer.
Perhaps paradoxically, English often teaches pupils about other cultures. We view having understanding and empathy for others as crucial, as is respecting our heritage. Knowing also that writers can change future society, Winchester provides leadership skills for a life in service to the wider world. Acquiring excellent communication skills is therefore a vital component of a Winchester education.
Discussion takes a central and highly anticipated role in every lesson. Dons are allowed the freedom to inspire their pupils with books that will resonate, not merely because they are on a syllabus – using texts that are not ‘set’, but ‘chosen’. Amongst the alumni are published novelists, editors, a film director, and a poet.
Students find fellowship in our Literary Societies and in producing school publications.
With a 13-strong department of native and non-native speakers, pupils are unlikely to be taught by the same don in two consecutive years. These differing approaches and areas of expertise ensure the pupils’ continuing enthusiasm in the subject. We push the top linguists and support the beginners, while increasing open-mindedness and knowledge of different cultures.
In addition to French being a great asset for many areas of the employment market, our course is designed to enhance critical skills in presentation and essay-writing. It also expands cultural knowledge of literature, cinema, drama, and history. High-achieving pupils have gone to French and Swiss universities, and we regularly send students to Oxford and Cambridge. Two pupils recently won the EU Translation Prize, Juvenes Translatores, whilst still at school.
Francophiles can also improve their fluency at our French Orpheus Glee Society.
We teach highly-focused lessons to get through the prescribed syllabus quickly. This then allows time to set extension reading tasks. Often these relate to current events or first-hand experience of the dons, such as farming, climate change and human migration. There is time too for the pupils to develop their natural curiosity via individual research, presenting their findings to the class and honing their verbal communication skills. A tacit respect between pupils and dons enables discussion that is relaxed and forthcoming.
Geography students become socially, environmentally, economically and politically aware, quickly seeing themselves as global citizens. Outside the classroom, we provide many opportunities to learn, with trips to observe post-glacial landscapes, fluvial geomorphology and microclimates, as well as paddle boarding in salt marshes and kayaking round the Jurassic Coast.
Practical humanitarianism continues in our many Vocational, Globally Cultural and Outdoors Clubs and Societies.
The study of German at Winchester is more than merely acquiring another language: it is the study of culture. Pupils explore a literary range that enhances and deepens their appreciation of Western culture and the arts. Yet the approach to language acquisition remains rigorous. By deconstructing German didactically, we strengthen language skills and achieve a level of learning beyond what is expected.
German is the most sought-after foreign language by UK employers, according to the CBI. Yet it is also a living language. Pupils enjoy adopting its idiosyncrasies and using them in and outside the classroom. Combining humour with hard work inspires the swift progress pupils make from first learning the language into their final year.
Talented linguists gain much from joining our German Play Reading Society.
During the first three years the study of History is combined with the other subjects in Div, and is thus studied by all pupils to Year 11, when it can also be taken as a GCSE. The curriculum ranges broadly. Pupils can expect to study aspects of the past from Classical Antiquity to the present day. The focus is on making lessons interesting and stimulating, allowing pupils to go beyond surface level discussion, and to engage in real depth with complex historical problems.
In Years 12 and 13, the Pre-U course allows dons the freedom to teach to their academic strengths and emphasises breadth as well as depth of learning. Outline papers in European and British history are designed to encourage a broad understanding of significant chronological periods, while the Special Subject and Personal Investigation allow pupils the opportunity to study specific topics in greater detail, with a focus on the use of primary sources. We offer three discrete periods, so pupils may choose to specialise in one of either the Medieval, Early Modern or Modern periods.
A wealth of artefacts to study and handle is available in the Archives, Fellows’ Library and Treasury.
Mathematics at Winchester is popular and exciting. The emphasis is on dialogue between the class and its teacher. This approach enables pupils to think critically and to challenge assumptions – many of our students go on to distinguished careers in the academic world and the Civil Service, as well as enjoying success in the City.
Results in public examinations are outstanding with over half our pupils leaving with A* equivalent in Mathematics and Further Mathematics.
Our various mathematical clubs prove popular, year on year, with pupils achieving success in UKMT competitions and supporting the local community.

Winchester College Launches First Virtual Look Inside New Sixth Form Girls Boarding House
From September 2026, Winchester College will welcome girl boarders in to its Sixth Form for the first time in its history.
To mark this historic moment, we have launched a virtual tour of the first girls boarding house to give a sense of what it might be like to be among its first residents.
Sixth Form Girls Boarding
Please accept cookies to enable video playback. Manage cookie settings
The two brand new girls boarding houses will be located next to the recently opened Winchester College Sports Centre. Both houses will have a mixture of single and double rooms, all with en-suites, a common room, dining hall and co-ed study spaces. All centred around a beautiful, spacious courtyard.
“Our dedicated pastoral team has been closely involved with the design of both buildings and the interiors”
Headmaster of Winchester College, Ms Elizabeth Stone commented: ‘Since we first announced our plan to welcome girls boarders into the Sixth Form at Winchester, we have been working hard to bring this vision to life. Our dedicated pastoral team, including house tutors, teachers, and health and wellbeing support staff, has been closely involved with the design of both buildings and the interiors. Their involvement has been to ensure that girls joining us in September 2026 receive a very warm welcome and will find a home they can be proud of, a space where they can thrive and create lasting memories during their two years with us.’
“Girls joining us in September 2026 will find a home they can be proud of, a space where they can thrive and create lasting memories during their two years with us.”

The Warden and Headmaster attend groundbreaking ceremony for new Sixth Form girls boarding houses
Members of the Governing Body, College community, guests from Winchester City Council and contractor, Gilbert Ash, gathered on Friday 3 May for the official groundbreaking ceremony for the two new Sixth Form girls boarding houses due to open in September 2026.
Welcoming guests to the ceremony, Sir Richard Stagg, Warden commented:
“This project began several years ago when we decided to welcome girls into the Sixth Form as boarders, so I’m delighted that today marks a significant practical milestone in bringing that project to life.”
He went on to say: ‘There have been many people involved in getting us to this point, including our friends at the City Council, as well as former Headmaster, Dr Tim Hands who guided the School through the early stages of the project. While the two houses will expand our school community, it is also our hope that it will increase our involvement with, and contribution to the City of Winchester.’
Raymond Gilroy, Construction Director at Gilbert Ash said: ‘We pride ourselves on close collaboration with our clients and delivering outstanding quality. We look forward to providing Winchester College with world class buildings future generations of pupils can be proud of.’

pageCache.pageTitle: A View On Adolescent Mental Health and Wellbeing - Winchester College | Independent Boarding School
pageCache.text:
A View On Adolescent Mental Health and Wellbeing
Headmaster, Ms Elizabeth Stone recently spoke to parents about adolescent mental health and wellbeing, informed by extensive research from Dr Jack Andrews, a Research Fellow at the University of Oxford in Developmental Science and Mental Health.
“The things we do to support pupil wellbeing are woven into the fabric of the school”
In her latest video, she commented: “The very best things we do at Winchester are not standalone programmes and campaigns or reactive, therapeutic responses. The things we do to support pupil wellbeing are woven into the fabric of the school. Developing true autonomy, competence and relatedness is what will set children up to withstand the knocks and bruises of daily life and help them come through the inevitable difficult and stressful periods a bit stronger, a bit wiser, more resilient, more confident and ultimately, happier.”
Hear more from the Headmaster in the video below.

pageCache.pageTitle: Launch of New Pupil-Led Academic Journal - Winchester College | Independent Boarding School
pageCache.text:
Launch of New Pupil-Led Academic Journal
We are glad to announce the publication of the first issue of Sapientia, the Academic Journal of Winchester College. The purpose of the journal is to be an alternative medium for pupils to share independent insights and academic findings that go beyond the confines of the curriculum and to highlight different fields of scholarship.
We are also aiming to maintain academic diversity. Although an emphasis on STEM subjects is definitely helpful and practical in our contemporary world, we would also like to give opportunities to students of the humanities and the social sciences to be well represented. We firmly believe that in an era where AI continues to grow and develop, humanities and social scientific research will take more prominence as we shift our focus back to the “human”.
In a sense, we hope that the journal encapsulates the conflicting age our generation dwells in: we were able to exploit the whole capacity of AI for image generation in our journal, yet our words and ideas are voices that are indubitably individual and unique.
We firmly believe that in an era where AI continues to grow and develop, humanities and social scientific research will take more prominence as we shift our focus back to the “human”.
In this issue we cover articles from various disciplines, including the social sciences, philosophy, and history, among others. Papers range from addressing the causes of financial crises, to the nature of elections, and also to comparative philosophical perspectives on universal themes like the self. Many articles were also put forward for submission in various other venues, most notably the John Locke Institute Global Essay Competition, where those that were submitted to the competition and published in the journal were all shortlisted.

Admissions
Academic Scholarships
For almost 650 years, Winchester has inspired intellectual curiosity and academic excellence. Through our academic scholarships, we support exceptional pupils who embody this spirit of enquiry and achievement.
Founder’s Scholarships
Founder’s Scholarships are prestigious awards that recognise academic excellence, intellectual curiosity, analytical rigour, and flexibility of mind.
Successful candidates receive a 25% reduction in school fees. Scholarships are awarded on merit and are not means-tested. They are available to new pupils joining the school in Year 9 and Year 12, and in the Sixth Form they are open to both day and boarding pupils.
Applicants may apply for both a Founder’s Scholarship and a means-tested bursary. These awards may be held simultaneously and are applied cumulatively. For example, a pupil awarded a 25% means-tested bursary and a 25% Founder’s Scholarship would receive a total fee remission of 50%.
Find out more
Scholars & Exhibitioners
Scholars and Exhibitioners join the school at 13+ having succeeded in Election, our academic scholarship examination.
Scholars board in College, the home of academic scholars at 13+, and are distinguished by the black gowns they wear. Exhibitioners join a boarding house rather than College.
These titles do not automatically include fee remission.
Election: a prestigious 13+ scholarship examination
The 13+ academic scholarship examination is known as ‘Election’. Election is taken instead of the Winchester Entrance exam and is a unique selection process involving both written examinations and interviews. Election typically takes place at the school over three days in the April or May of Year 8.
This year, the Election papers will take place on Monday 27th, Tuesday 28th, and Wednesday 29th of April 2026.
You can find out more information about Election here
Those pupils who are successful at Election are awarded either:
A Scholarship – pupils are offered a place to board in College and on joining the school, they are known as Scholars and are distinguished by the gowns they wear.
An Exhibition – pupils are publicly recognised for their academic ability and accept their existing offer of a place in one of the school’s other boarding houses.
The top performers in Election are offered Founder’s Scholarships.
An Academic Scholarship or Exhibition does not automatically carry a remission of school fees. Financial assistance is available via our substantial bursaries programme.
The Election process begins at the end of year 7 or the beginning of year 8 when boys and their families who are interested in considering Election visit College. These visits will include lunch with the ‘Collegemen’, a tour around College and a meeting with the Master-in-College. Successful candidates will then be invited to Election.
As part of Election, candidates will have two separate interviews, one with the Master-in-College and one with a member of the College’s Academic Senior Leadership Team. The interviews are designed to identify scholarly qualities through conversation.
Candidates from prep schools take required papers in English, Maths 1, Science and General Paper 1, plus at least three optional papers from the following subjects Latin, French, Greek, History, Geography, Maths 2 and General Paper 2.
Candidates from the maintained sector must take English, Maths 1 and General Paper 1, but may choose additional subjects.
The syllabuses for Maths and English (which are common to both the Entrance and the Election exams) are below.
Specimen papers are helpful in providing an indication of the level and difficulty of typical questions in the Election exams. Each year, a lot of work goes into developing new papers which are designed purely to test scholarly thinking, rather than testing revised or rehearsed answers.
To find out more about applying for Election, or to arrange a visit and meet the Master-in-College Dr Latter, please contact the College and Election Secretary, Mrs Ros Robertson.

pageCache.text:
Performing Arts at Yateley Manor
The Performing Arts are a vibrant and much-loved part of school life at Yateley Manor. From class assemblies and LAMDA examinations to whole-school productions, every pupil is encouraged to take part and express themselves.
Drama and Performance
Drama encourages imagination, empathy and teamwork. Many pupils choose to take LAMDA exams, which develop confidence and clarity in communication.
Each year, pupils take part in a range of performances – from imaginative class plays to full-scale productions in our drama studio. The Yateley Manor Youth Theatre and Youth Dance groups offer additional opportunities to perform and collaborate creatively.
Dance
Dance is taught from the earliest years, with Ballet available in Pre-Prep and a broad range of modern and contemporary classes as pupils move up the school. Through the performing arts, pupils learn not just how to perform, but how to present themselves with assurance, creativity and joy.

Facilities
How to Book Yateley Manor's Facilities
Our facilities, which include the sports hall, swimming pool and pitches as well as Drama Studio, Gym, Music School and Manor Place Hall, are available for hire, either by clubs and organisations or by individuals. Used regularly by local sports clubs and interest groups, we have also hosted events ranging from bridal fairs to national chess competitions. To view our full range of available facilities, please scroll down the page. To book any our our first class facilities we have on offer, please click the button below
Why should you book Yateley Manor's Facilities?
Children need space to learn and at Yateley Manor our extensive grounds provide the perfect facilities to inspire and challenge every child. The Creative Arts and Languages Centre provides state-of-the-art facilities in bright and spacious classrooms. The Music Technology Suite allows children to produce digital music with keyboards connected to computers and the six practice rooms provide ample space for individual and group rehearsals.
The indoor swimming pool is in use all year round. Behind Manor House and Manor Court, the main school building, the spacious sports hall, with its impressive cricket nets, football, netball and basketball facilities, is complemented by a second gymnasium and numerous sports pitches.Imaginatively equipped play areas give children the freedom to unwind and play creatively. There are a whole host of physical activities to try, including Dance and Ballet in our specially equipped Studio.
Opportunities to use the Berry Cooking Centre are timetabled regularly. Younger children learn how to cook basic meals and understand good food hygiene whilst older children cook across the curriculum in different subjects. This includes preparing food using rationing principles in History lessons and having a complete lesson taught in French, with oral instructions and recipes in the language.
Outdoor learning can boost children’s welfare and their performance at school. Spending time interacting with nature can boost children’s creativity and problem-solving skills. Our Woodland Learning Area has been designed to capitalise on these benefits and, together with the expertise of fully trained staff, the facility really brings out a different side of children.
A climbing wall and an Aeroball frame are popular recent additions to our facilities both donated by FYMS (Friends of Yateley Manor School).
What facilities do we have available to book?
Fyson Blum Hall
Our large modern sports hall is equipped with four full size indoor cricket net bays suitable for use with a hard ball.
The hall also has floor markings for
The Hall is also used for concerts and assemblies and has a seating capacity for 400 people and a large AV screen.
4 badminton courts
5-a-side football court with goals
short tennis
Swimming Pool
The swimming pool is a 16 metre indoor teaching pool which has a depth of 0.8m at one end and 1.5m at the other end and is ideally suited to teaching young children. It can be divided into three sections across the pool or four lanes and the school regularly hosts swimming galas. The pool is heated to a comfortable 86 degrees Fahrenheit (30 degrees Celsius) and is also used for kayak practice.
Gymnasium
The gymnasium has a resilient floor and is equipped with mini gymnastic equipment.
It is regularly hired out for activities such as martial arts, exercise classes and dance classes.
Studio
The studio is a small theatre/dance studio and is used for dance clubs and small productions. It has a raised area at one end and adjustable staging at the other. It also has a ballet barre on two walls and can seat 100 people.
Manor Place Hall
A multi-purpose hall with AV screen located in the Manor Place building. It is used for a variety of activities including music recitals and performances, presentations and workshops.
It is also ideal for hiring for dance or exercise classes, parties and martial arts. A small kitchenette and toilets are located just off the hall and tables and chairs are also available.
Music School and Tech Suite
The new Music School affords a large teaching room and six bright and airy practice rooms as well as a separate percussion room. A music technology suite allows pupils to use keyboards to record pieces into computers for manipulation through the software.
Berry (Cookery Room)
Being able to cook is a life skill and yet it is a skill which is becoming more and more marginalised in schools. At Yateley Manor we are passionate about preparing children for adult lives and cookery is one such skill. Basic cookery starts in our Nursery classes and children develop an awareness of hygiene and cookery utensils as they move through Pre Prep classes. In later years children use the facility to broaden and contextualise their learning across the curriculum, such as cooking in language and science lessons.
The Cuisine Centre can accommodate a class comfortably, with individual sinks and ovens. Our MasterChef clubs after school are very popular.
No matter how proficient a child is at cookery, they will enjoy the practical nature of cookery and enjoy the end results.
Fields and Pitches
Yateley Manor has a range of courts and outside grass areas which can be used for netball, tennis, hockey, rounders, cricket, rugby or football depending on the season. In the summer the fields are also set out for athletics including a five lane 300m grass running track and long jump pit.

pageCache.pageTitle: Senior School at Yateley Manor | Years 7-9
pageCache.text:
Senior School at Yateley Manor
It’s where pupils evolve — often transforming from quiet observers into confident young people who feel ready to take centre stage in their learning and school life. Our aim is to ensure every pupil flourishes across these years: academically, socially and personally.
Manor Place & Senior Hub
A dedicated Senior base with study areas, lockers and social spaces designed to support focus, friendship and self-reliance.
Specialist Classrooms & Labs
Fully equipped science, design and computing facilities allow pupils to experiment, innovate and explore ideas in depth
Sport & Fitness Facilities
Exceptional pitches, courts and a fitness suite provide the setting for teamwork, resilience and a lifelong love of sport.
Creative & Performing Arts Spaces
From music rooms and drama studios to art and DT workshops, our creative facilities encourage imagination and expression.
Years 7 & 8 – A Formative Stage
These early senior years are full of opportunity and development. Specialist teaching becomes the norm, enabling pupils to deepen skills across subjects with renewed focus and ambition. Pupils continue to hone foundational skills through the Prep School Baccalaureate core programme while exploring new horizons — enquiries, challenges and creative tasks become central to everyday learning.
Small tutor groups foster strong relationships with staff, enabling personal guidance and mutual respect. The focus is as much on character and confidence as it is on academic progress.
Beyond the Classroom
Trips & Expeditions
Where learning meets the real world. From Normandy to New Scientist Live, fieldwork and residential trips broaden horizons and deepen understanding far beyond the classroom.
Enrichment and Leadership
Where confidence and character take centre stage. Through mentoring, school committees and ambassador roles, seniors learn to lead, collaborate and make a lasting contribution.
Sport and Challenge
Where resilience and teamwork thrive. A dynamic sports programme, academies and competitions inspire every pupil to push boundaries, play fair and perform with pride.
Creative and Performing Arts
Where imagination becomes expression. From concerts and productions to art and design showcases, senior pupils develop creative confidence and the courage to perform.
Looking Ahead – The Path to GCSE
At Yateley Manor, we challenge pupils to aim high. For many, Years 7-9 lay the groundwork for their GCSE years (10-11). With our forward-thinking outlook, we already offer GCSE options in subjects such as PE to younger pupils, showcasing our commitment to stretching each individual.
Our growing Senior School is built around high academic standards, small class sizes and outstanding teaching — all underpinned by a culture of care and opportunity.
Pastoral Care
Every pupil in our Senior School is encouraged to take on responsibility beyond the classroom. Whether helping lead their class to assembly, supporting peers during break times or acting as a tour guide for prospective families, these experiences help shape confident, articulate young people. Our strong pastoral structure, with small tutor groups and dedicated staff, ensures each pupil is supported as they grow in capability and independence.
Clubs and Activities
Discover Yateley Manor’s wide range of co-curricular clubs and activities. From sport and art to music, design, and outdoor adventures — there’s something for everyone.
Visit Yateley Manor
Whether you’re just starting your school search or looking for the right fit for your child, we’d love to welcome you.

From the earliest years, pupils are encouraged to sing, perform and explore their creativity through a wide range of musical experiences. Pre-Prep at Yateley Manor School
At Yateley Manor our Pre-Prep children flourish in a setting that combines stimulating learning with genuine care. Our aim is to enable each child to become a confident, well-educated individual with a lifelong enthusiasm for learning.
A Welcoming Learning Environment
Our Pre-Prep classrooms are bright, welcoming and full of opportunity. Each class is led by a dedicated class teacher, supported by a full-time teaching assistant, ensuring that children feel known, supported and engaged through a broad range of activities and subjects that make learning fun.
Building the Essentials
As children move into Year 1 and Year 2, we emphasise growing independence alongside academic progress. Daily phonics sessions, regular guided reading and a strong focus on writing and number work provide a firm foundation. Children are expected to be heard reading by an adult regularly, reinforcing confidence and fluency.
Connected Curriculum
Our curriculum is thoughtfully designed so learning is purposeful and interconnected. Topics link across subjects to give meaning and context, while discrete lessons — for example in mathematics and phonics — provide targeted teaching. Specialist subject teachers contribute to areas such as swimming and sport through our Games department.
Specialist Teaching & Broad Horizons
Even in Pre-Prep, children benefit from specialist teaching. Whether learning French, developing coordination in dance or improving fitness in PE, the experience is rich and varied. Every day brings an opportunity to build new skills and explore fresh interests.
Pastoral Care
At Yateley Manor Pre-Prep, pastoral care is woven into every part of school life. Our teachers take the time to know each child as an individual — their interests, their worries and what makes them shine. We create a safe, nurturing environment where children feel secure, valued and understood, building the confidence and resilience that will support them throughout their educational journey.
Looking Ahead to Prep School
At Yateley Manor, every child’s journey builds naturally from one stage to the next. As children move from Pre-Prep to Prep School, they take with them curiosity, confidence and a love of learning – ready to explore new subjects, develop independence and discover their individual strengths. In Prep, specialist teaching, wider opportunities and a nurturing environment ensure each child continues to thrive – academically, socially and personally — preparing them for the exciting years ahead

pageCache.pageTitle: Prep School at Yateley Manor | Years 3-6
pageCache.text:
Prep School at Yateley
As children join Yateley Manor in Years 3–6, our transition and pastoral arrangements are designed to welcome them quickly and securely into our school family. From the very start, new pupils feel recognised, supported and ready to flourish. Our aim is to develop happy, confident children who love learning. We celebrate each individual’s talents and achievements, while also nurturing areas for growth. By following this philosophy, our pupils become independent, self-assured young learners - prepared for the next phase of their journey.
Academic Spaces
Specialist classrooms and science labs designed to spark discovery and nurture a lifelong love of learning.
Creative Studios
From art and design to music and drama, our creative spaces encourage expression, confidence and collaboration.
Sport & Performance
Modern sports facilities and performance areas inspire children to challenge themselves, play with passion and celebrate every success.
Outdoor Learning & Wellbeing
Expansive grounds, adventure areas and calm corners provide space to think, explore and build resilience together.
Year 3 & 4
In Years 3 and 4, children are based in their own section of the school where classrooms are closely linked, creating a strong sense of community within their year group.
Pupils benefit from access to the full range of school facilities including -Art, Cookery, French and Music -helping them explore a wide variety of interests from early on.
Children are encouraged to participate in sport and begin inter-school matches, while their learning environment remains creative, nurturing and full of opportunity. We aim to provide school days that are vibrant and full of new experiences — from visiting ancient Celtic farms to imaginative role-play with a Roman legionnaire.
Year 5 & 6
As pupils move into Years 5 and 6, their learning accelerates in a setting shaped for growing independence and focus. In every subject, lessons are taught by specialists and pupils move around campus, gaining experience of different teaching styles, classrooms and learning contexts.
For those pupils moving on to senior schools at the end of Year 6, we offer a thorough support programme to help prepare them for entry examinations — ensuring they move forward with confidence and readiness.
Beyond the Classroom
Trips and Visits
Where learning leaps off the page. From museums and field studies to immersive history days, every trip brings subjects to life through adventure and experience.
Clubs & Activities
Where passions are discovered and talents grow. A rich programme of lunchtime and after-school clubs helps children try new things, build confidence, and follow their curiosity.
Outdoor Learning
Where challenges build character. Children explore nature, teamwork and leadership through forest activities, fieldwork and residential trips that inspire independence.
Performing Arts & Expression
Where every voice finds its stage. Music, drama and dance give children the freedom to perform, collaborate and shine with confidence.
Pastoral Care
Pastoral care is strong across the Prep School and becomes especially evident in Years 5 and 6. Tutor groups are small (typically around ten pupils), and the Form Tutor remains with the group for two years, supporting continuity of relationships, trust and understanding. The Form Tutor is the first point of contact for pastoral matters, though parents are welcome to engage with subject teachers directly for more specific discussions.
Looking Ahead to Senior School
As children move through Yateley Manor’s Prep School, they grow in independence, curiosity and confidence – ready to embrace the challenges and opportunities of Senior life. With specialist teaching, leadership roles and a rich co-curricular programme, pupils develop the skills, values and self-belief that prepare them for success in the years ahead. The transition to Senior School feels seamless – a continuation of the same supportive community where every child is known, encouraged and inspired to reach their potential

Working at Yateley Manor
At Yateley Manor, working here means joining more than a team — it means becoming part of a community built on respect, encouragement and shared purpose. We believe that strong relationships between staff and pupils are the cornerstone of our success, and we aim to support every member of our team in both professional growth and personal fulfilment.From the moment you arrive, you’ll find an environment where your ideas are heard, your development is prioritised and your role contributes meaningfully to pupils’ lives. Regular professional development, peer collaboration and a warm culture of support ensure that every colleague can thrive.
Whether you are a teacher, a member of our support staff, or part of our Early Years or holiday-camp teams, you will find purpose, challenge and reward in the work you do. At Yateley Manor we celebrate each other’s successes, encourage continuous improvement and look forward together to what pupils can achieve. Join us and find more than a job — find a place where your ambition, kindness and expertise are valued.
What our staff say
Our staff often tell us that Yateley Manor feels like much more than a workplace - it feels like a community where they are known, appreciated and able to contribute.
“I feel supported to try new ideas in my teaching and know that the whole team will back me.”
“Being part of Yateley Manor means being part of something special — the relationships with colleagues and pupils make such a difference.”
– Support Staff Member
Their experiences reflect a culture in which colleagues grow together, learn together and achieve together. Professional development is ongoing, with internal workshops, mentoring and opportunities for leadership roles. Every role at Yateley Manor is valued and every voice matters.

Little Lodge Nursery at Yateley Manor School
At Little Lodge Nursery, every day is an adventure in learning and discovery. We provide a happy, nurturing environment where curiosity is encouraged, friendships flourish, and children feel confident to explore the world around them.
A message from our Nursery Manager
“From the moment I first stepped into Little Lodge, I knew it was a special place. The warmth of the children, the kindness of the staff and the sense of joy in every room made me feel instantly at home.
My passion has always been to give children the best possible start in life — helping them to grow in confidence, develop independence and love learning from the very beginning.”
Miss Kirsty Cordery Nursery Manager, Little Lodge Nursery
Trusted by Local Families
What Sets Little Lodge Apart
Our youngest learners benefit from Yateley Manor’s exceptional facilities, including access to the Woodland School, the school gym and the theatre for performances and assemblies.
What Sets Little Lodge Apart
Specialist teachers introduce children to subjects such as French, Dance and Physical Education, sparking curiosity and laying the foundations for future learning.
What Sets Little Lodge Apart
Our nursery has been thoughtfully designed to provide bright, well-equipped rooms and a large, imaginative outdoor play area -perfect for exploration, creativity and fun.
What Sets Little Lodge Apart
Little Lodge pupils are an important part of our wider school family. Older pupils often visit to read stories, help with activities and join in with events such as sports days, creating a strong sense of connection across the age groups.
What Sets Little Lodge Apart
When the time comes to move on, children are exceptionally well prepared for Reception. We offer transition mornings and parent information sessions to ensure the process feels calm, familiar and exciting. For families moving to other schools, our team provides support and guidance every step of the way.
Useful Information
Settling In
Starting nursery is a big step – for children and parents alike. To help every child feel comfortable, we offer three settling-in sessions during the week before their start date.
The first session includes a meeting with your child’s key person, with parents staying for 30 minutes before leaving briefly.
The following two sessions are completed independently by the child, helping them build confidence and familiarity. Further information about our settling-in process is available upon request.
Parent Communication
We value strong partnerships with parents. Each child has a personal online learning journal through Family, where parents can view daily updates on their child’s learning, care routines and achievements. Parents can also message their child’s key worker directly at any time. Additional nursery news is shared weekly through our parent newsletter, INAMOS.
Transition to Reception
Children moving into Reception enjoy a smooth, supported transition. During the summer term, they take part in three settling-in sessions with the Reception team, meeting teachers and current pupils while exploring their new classroom environment.
This thoughtful approach ensures children begin the next stage of their journey happy, confident and ready to shine.
Fees & Admissions
To find out our current fee structure, register entrance or arrange a nursery visit, please contact the Nursery Office using the enquiry form below.

Our Values
The values of our school are like a heartbeat for everybody. Values guide our actions, so they are in alignment with our beliefs. They also connect us to the core of who we are. At Yateley Manor we have six core values which run through our community. They help guide the way we are with one another; they channel our behaviour and bring the community together to provide children with opportunities which will lead to successful adult lives.
Happiness
Happiness means finding joy and satisfaction in everyday life. It looks different for everyone, but it always involves positivity, gratitude, and a sense of fulfilment. Even in challenging times, happy people hold onto optimism – trusting that they can overcome difficulties and find joy again.
Reflectiveness
Being reflective allows us to learn deeply and meaningfully. Reflection helps us make sense of our experiences, connecting what we learn in the classroom with the world around us. It builds insight, understanding and a lifelong curiosity for learning.
Community
Community is at the heart of who we are. It gives us a sense of belonging, shared purpose and pride. At Yateley Manor, everyone matters – each individual contributes to the spirit, character and strength of our community.
Resilience
Resilience is the strength to keep going when things don’t go to plan. It helps us face challenges, learn from setbacks and find enjoyment in life. Resilient people don’t see failure as defeat, but as an opportunity to grow and improve.
Teamwork
Teamwork is about working together towards a shared goal. It brings out the best in everyone by combining different strengths, ideas and perspectives. Learning to collaborate effectively is a vital skill that children carry with them throughout life.
Relationships
Strong relationships are the foundation of a thriving school. They inspire motivation, nurture confidence and create a sense of trust and belonging. At Yateley Manor, our relationships – between children and adults alike – are built on care, challenge, support and mutual respect.

pageCache.pageTitle: Academics at Yateley Manor School. Curiosity, Confidence and Character
pageCache.text:
Academics at Yateley Manor
We believe every child should feel inspired to think independently, ask questions and enjoy the process of discovery. Our journey begins in Nursery and continues through to Senior School, with each stage designed to stretch, support and celebrate every pupil.
Our curriculum goes beyond the National Curriculum. As an independent school we are free to design a rich programme of learning that connects subjects, brings real-world relevance and invites deeper thinking. For example, children may code a computer game and create its soundtrack or explore 3D art inspired by everyday materials.
Small class sizes and specialist teachers ensure that every pupil receives the attention and challenge they need. The result is more than excellent examination outcomes: it is a child who leaves us ready for whatever comes next, with confidence, intellectual curiosity and strong character.
Attitude to Learning
At Yateley Manor we believe that how a child learns is as important as what they learn. We measure and nurture the ‘attitude to learning’ through key indicators such as engagement, preparation, punctuality and perseverance.
Our four-point grading system for Attitude to Learning (A–D) is a clear framework for improvement. Grades are recorded every four weeks so that families stay informed about both academic progress and the learning behaviours that underpin success.
The focus on learning behaviours means pupils develop beyond the classroom: they learn to collaborate effectively, ask for support when needed, stay focused during a task and reflect on their own progress. This builds resilient, self-aware learners who carry their growth mindset into Senior School and beyond.
Preparing for life beyond the classroom
Qualifications remain important, but we know they are not everything. At Yateley Manor we educate the whole child -academic, practical, creative and personal. We support pupils to become not just high achievers but people of integrity, self-confidence and purpose.
From the earliest years to the final year, children are encouraged to take ownership of their learning. They learn to reflect, adapt and improve. At Senior level, they often lead in school life, present to different audiences and take responsibility for their environment.
Why it Matters
By the time our pupils leave Yateley Manor, they are well-prepared for the next stage of their education -but more than that, they are ready to learn for life. They have honed the habits of mind and the confidence to thrive in unfamiliar environments, to take part in debate, to initiate ideas and to be resilient in the face of challenge.
